paper_title: DreamX: Video Diffusion Model is a Universal Latent Action Learner

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.

sections.content: DREAMX: VIDEO DIFFUSION MODEL IS UNIVERSAL LATENT ACTION LEARNER Jisoo Kim1 Chaehyun Kim1 Eunbeen Hong1 Soowon Son1 1KAIST Project page: https://cvlab-kaist.github.io/DreamX Junsu Kim1 Fu-En Yang2 Jiho Park1 Seungryong Kim1 2NVIDIA Seongchan Kim Figure 1: DreamX learns shared action interface from egocentric human videos and robot videos. Compact, embodiment-agnostic latent actions extracted from pretrained video diffusion model capture motion consistently across changes in embodiment and scene appearance. The same representation enables transferring motion from source video to target video, decoding human motion into executable robot actions without paired humanrobot training data, and training lightweight latent policy that jointly predicts latent actions and robot actions.

sections.content: Learning universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Generalist robot policies, including vision-language-action (VLA) models (Kim et al., 2024; Bjorck et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2025) and world action models (WAMs) (Kim et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026), benefit from diverse robot demonstrations, but collecting such data at scale remains costly. Human egocentric videos offer promising alternative as scalable source of diverse manipulation behaviors, and recent works leverage these videos for policy learning (Li et al., 2025; Kareer et al., 2025). However, action supervision remains tied to the embodiment that produces it. Human videos lack robot action labels, and even robot demonstrations use different control spaces across embodiments. The same behavior can therefore correspond to different low-level actions, making action labels difficult to share directly across embodiments. Overcoming this mismatch calls for common action representation that preserves shared motion and effects across embodiments. Latent action models (LAMs) offer promising route toward learning such representation from video. Although humans and robots have different bodies and control spaces, their actions can all be observed as changes in visual scene. LAMs typically use dedicated encoders to compress these changes into compact representations, called latent actions (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025c; Bu et al., 2025b), where these encoders are trained using decoder that reconstructs future frames solely from the current frame and latent actions. However, reconstruction accuracy alone does not ensure that latent actions isolate the underlying action. The learned representations can also encode domain-specific visual information, such as viewpoint and scene appearance, whenever it helps reconstruction (Nikulin et al., 2025). Capturing action-relevant structure shared across embodiments while separating it from domain-specific visual factors therefore remains challenge. Pretrained video diffusion models provide promising foundation for addressing this challenge. First, through large-scale video generation, they learn rich spatiotemporal representations that capture motion, correspondence, geometry, and semantic structure (Nam et al., 2026; Wiedemer et al., 2025; Son et al., 2025). Such representations encode how scenes, objects, and agents evolve over time, making them natural source of action-relevant dynamics. Second, these models possess generative prior that enables future-frame synthesis conditioned on an initial frame and an additional signal. With scene appearance supplied by the initial frame, additional conditioning can guide how the scene evolves. Together, these priors motivate extracting latent actions directly from pretrained spatiotemporal representations and supervising their learning with pretrained generative decoder. We introduce DreamX, framework for learning universal latent actions across embodiments using pretrained video diffusion model. We pass learnable query tokens alongside the video tokens through the models spatiotemporal attention, allowing the queries to gather action-relevant information across frames. The queries condense frame-to-frame changes represented by 1,200 frame tokens into just 4 latent-action tokens, yielding 300 reduction in token count. These latent actions replace text conditioning in the same model to reconstruct future frames from the initial frame. With scene appearance supplied by the initial frame and visual detail by the pretrained generative prior, the reconstruction objective encourages latent actions to capture the motion needed to explain the observed future. Trained on heterogeneous human and robot videos, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models on LARYBench (Nie et al., 2026) and enables any-to-any video transfer and human-to-robot action transfer without paired training data. As downstream application, we also show that the learned latent actions can serve as prediction targets for an observationconditioned robot policy, without requiring future-video generation during execution. Together, these results suggest that DreamX learns shared, transferable latent action space that supports motion transfer across embodiments and can also serve as basis for downstream policy learning. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We introduce DreamX, framework that uses the spatiotemporal and generative priors of pretrained video diffusion model to learn universal latent actions. The resulting representations achieve state-of-the-art performance among latent action models on LARYBench. We demonstrate that the learned latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and humanto-robot action transfer without paired sourcetarget training data. We further show the use of compact latent-action codes as prediction targets for downstream policy learning.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Latent action models. Latent action models (LAMs) learn action representations from visual transitions, enabling action-unlabeled videos to supervise downstream control. LAPO (Schmidt & Jiang, 2024) and Genie (Bruce et al., 2024) established the paradigm, recovering discrete latent actions through an inverseforward dynamics bottleneck over adjacent frames. LAPA (Ye et al., 2025) further scales this recipe for vision-language-action pretraining, and Moto (Chen et al., 2025c) tokenizes visual motion for manipulation. Later work incorporates additional cues: UniVLA (Bu et al., 2025b) grounds latent actions with semantic visual features, villa-X (Chen et al., 2025b) integrates language and robot-state dynamics, and CoMo (Yang et al., 2026) and DiLA (Zhang et al., 2026) separate motion from visual content. Across these variants, the action space is learned from scratch on local visual transition, often single frame pair. Such supervision offers no view of how motion persists beyond one step, so the encoder entangles action with appearance and yields representations tied to their training embodiments. Emergent capabilities of video generative models. Video generative models acquire spatiotemporal structure by modeling how scenes evolve over time. Their internal representations support correspondence, point tracking, optical flow, and geometric understanding without task-specific supervision (Nam et al., 2026; Velez et al., 2025; Vedder et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025), and text-conditioned models further exhibit semantic grounding over objects, behaviors, and interactions (Wiedemer et al., 2025). Rather than encoding physical laws explicitly, these representations capture motion, geometry, and semantics jointly: which entities are present, where they are, and how they move over time. This is precisely the composition latent action must express, which is structured change of specific entity in specific place, and it is acquired from web-scale video rather than from single frame pair. Video generative priors for latent action learning. Recent work connects these two lines. VPP (Hu et al., 2024) conditions manipulation policy on the predictive visual representations inside fine-tuned video diffusion model, but still learns the policy from action labels. AdaWorld (Gao et al., 2025) learns latent actions for adaptable video prediction, and VideoWorld2 (Ren et al., 2026b) pairs pretrained video diffusion model for generation with separate latent dynamics model. In both, the video model acts as generative prior supplying pixels or rollouts, while the action representation is produced by an external module trained from scratch on frame-level transitions. Thus, the latent action encoder does not directly read the video diffusion backbones internal representations. We instead read latent actions directly from the models rich spatiotemporal representation, making maximal use of video pretraining and requiring no per-embodiment action encoder.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: Given video and instruction, DreamX uses learnable queries to extract compact latent actions from pretrained video diffusion backbones spatiotemporal features. Future-frame reconstruction conditioned on these latent actions and the initial frame provides generative supervision (Sec. 3.2). The learned representation enables video and action transfer with target initial frame or robot state (Sec. 3.3). For control, the DreamX policy predicts compact codes and low-level actions without generating future video (Sec. 3.4). 3.1 PRELIMINARIES: VIDEO DIFFUSION MODELS We build on Cosmos-Predict2.5 (Ali et al., 2025), pretrained video diffusion transformer. causal video autoencoder compresses clip into latent frames, = (V0, . . . , VN 1), where V0 encodes only the initial frame. These frames are patchified into spatial tokens and jointly modeled through spatiotemporal attention. Through video pretraining, the model learns spatiotemporal priors that capture spatial context and temporal relationships across the clip. Conditioned on an initial frame and an additional signal such as text, collectively denoted by c, the model learns future-video generation through flow matching. Given clean video latents and noise ϵ (0, I), we form xτ = (1 τ )x + τ ϵ, with τ [0, 1], and minimize Lvideo = Ex,c,ϵ,τ (cid:104) vθ(xτ , τ ; c) (ϵ x)2 2 (cid:105) , (1) where vθ predicts the flow velocity. 3 Figure 2: DreamX architecture and attention masks. (a) Learnable queries read out the pretrained video backbones spatiotemporal representations to encode latent actions. decoder initialized from the same pretrained backbone reconstructs future video from the latent actions and the initial frame, with auxiliary action supervision when labels are available. (b) Encoder and decoder attention masks control information flow among video, query, and action tokens. In the decoder, video and action tokens read the latent-action queries but do not attend to one another. By optimizing this objective over large-scale video data, the model acquires generative prior over scene appearance and plausible dynamics. When the initial frame supplies the scenes appearance, additional conditioning steers how the scene evolves. We exploit this property by using latent actions to steer future-frame reconstruction, whose objective supervises what the latent actions encode. 3.2 LEARNING UNIVERSAL LATENT ACTIONS FROM VIDEO DIFFUSION PRIORS DreamX adapts pretrained video diffusion backbone for two complementary roles: encoding observed dynamics into latent actions and supervising them through future-frame reconstruction to encourage separation of motion from visual appearance. Building on Sec. 3.1, we introduce learnable queries that read out the video representations to summarize observed dynamics as latent actions, while the decoder reconstructs the future from these latent actions and the initial frame. Leveraging video diffusion backbone for both the encoder and decoder allows its generative prior to account for visual appearance, encouraging the latent action tokens to focus on motion. Latent Action Encoding from Spatiotemporal Dynamics. DreamX uses pretrained video model itself to encode latent actions. As shown in Figure 2(a), we append learnable query tokens to the video token sequence and process them jointly through the backbones spatiotemporal attention. We assign group of query tokens qg to each latent frame Vg. Once contextualized by the video, their output features form the latent-action group Qg. All groups are extracted in single forward, = Eϕ(q; V, ℓ), (2) where Eϕ() is the encoder and ℓ is the language instruction supplied through the backbones original cross-attention. As shown in Figure 2(b), query-to-video attention is frame-causal, so Qg directly attends to V0:g, while query-to-query attention is unrestricted. This lets the queries encode temporally grounded motion from the pretrained dynamics, with query-layout settings in Appendix A.2. Generative Decoding for Action-Centric Latent Learning. Encoding from video alone may retain sceneand embodiment-specific visual cues. We therefore use the same pretrained video backbone as the encoder to supervise latent actions through future-frame reconstruction, conditioned on V0 and Q0:N 1 without text. As V0 provides scene appearance and the pretrained generative prior captures plausible evolution, is encouraged to encode the motion needed to explain the future, rather than visual cues already available to the decoder. As shown in Figure 2(a), the decoder Dθ() generates future frames conditioned on Q0:N 1, concatenated with the video tokens along the temporal sequence. This capability emerges from the pretraining described in the previous section and requires no additional training. The auxiliary robot action branch further encourages the latent actions to encode action-relevant cues and further enables motion extracted from source video to be decoded into continuous actions executable by target embodiment. Given source video, we extract its latent actions using the frozen DreamX encoder, Qsrc = Eϕ(q; Vsrc, ℓsrc), which captures the motion to be transferred. As shown in Figure 3(a), we reuse the same Qsrc in two complementary ways. For video transfer, we combine it with target initial frame tgt and use the frozen DreamX decoder Dθ to generate target video that reproduces the source motion under the target scene and embodiment. Whereas motion transfer uses latent actions extracted from source demonstration, the policy predicts them from the current observation and instruction. To this end, we repurpose the same pretrained video backbone used by DreamX to predict latent actions in place of future video (Kim et al., 2026a). Although is compact in token count, each token retains the full backbone width, making direct diffusion high-dimensional (Chen et al., 2025a). With the DreamX encoder frozen, we train the bottleneck using feature reconstruction and KL regularization. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
sections.content: We evaluate whether DreamX learns universal latent actions by examining how well they capture motion (Sec. 4.1) and whether they can transfer across scenes and embodiments (Secs. 4.24.3). We further assess their utility for learning effective and efficient policies from human and robot demonstrations (Sec. 4.4), followed by ablations and analysis of the learned representation (Secs. 4.54.6). Implementation details. We instantiate DreamX with Cosmos-Predict2.5 2B and pretrain on robot demonstrations from MolmoAct2-BimanualYAM (Fang et al., 2026), Bridge (Walke et al., 2023), DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024), and AgiBot (Bu et al., 2025a), together with human videos from EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2026) and EgoVerse (Punamiya et al., 2026). Videos are processed at 480 640 resolution with variable-length clips of up to 29 frames. We assign four query tokens to each VAE latent frame. We adapt the encoder and decoder using separate rank-16 LoRA modules for 78,000 training steps. Further training details are provided in Appendix A.2. 4.1 REPRESENTATION QUALITY We examine how well DreamXs latent actions capture motion on LARYBench (Nie et al., 2026). Regression asks whether the representation retains enough fine-grained motion to recover endeffector trajectories, and classification whether it carries enough semantic information to distinguish different motions. Table 1 compares DreamX with latent action models that encode either frame pairs or video clips. DreamX achieves the best performance across all benchmarks. Compared with the strongest baseline, DiLA, DreamX reduces regression MSE from 0.38 to 0.17 and increases classification accuracy from 62.25% to 69.67%. These results support leveraging video models as source of action-relevant representations: reading latent actions directly from their pretrained priors yields representations that capture spatial, temporal, and semantic structure across embodiments. FAE-32, our 32-channel compressed representation (Sec. 3.4), also outperforms all baselines, indicating that even the compact codes retain substantial motion and semantic information. Further evaluation details are provided in Appendix B.4. 6 Figure 4: Qualitative Any-to-Any video transfer. Each example shows source motion and the corresponding transferred video generated from target-domain initial observation. These results demonstrate that the learned latent action transfers motion across substantial changes in embodiment and scene appearance. Blue dots indicate the end-effector trajectory throughout the video frames. 4.2 VIDEO TRANSFER We evaluate whether DreamX learns universal latent actions by transferring source motion across scenes and embodiments while preserving the appearance specified by target initial frame. We examine any-to-any video transfer and quantitatively evaluate zero-shot human-to-robot transfer. Zeroshot evaluation details and additional transfer examples are provided in Appendices B.5 and D.1. Any-to-any video transfer. Figure 4 shows motion transfer across environments for the same robot, between different robot embodiments, and from humans to robots, with DAVIS example extending beyond manipulation. DreamX reproduces the source motion while preserving the target scene and embodiment. These results support the universality of the learned latent actions across embodiments and environments, extending to general-domain videos. Zero-shot human-to-robot transfer. We evaluate zero-shot human-to-robot transfer on HumanAndRobot (Xie et al., 2026), comparing with AdaWorld (Gao et al., 2025) and VideoWorld 2 (Ren et al., 2026b), both of which use diffusionbased video decoders. Paired robot recordings serve only as evaluation references; no paired humanrobot data is used for training. DreamX outperforms both baselines on every metric in Table 2 and follows the source human motion while preserving the target robot and scene (Figure 5). In contrast, Table 2: Zero-shot human-torobot video transfer on H&R. DreamX outperforms baselines across all metrics without paired humanrobot training data. AdaWorld 170.19 0.344 VideoWorld2 241.92 0.299 0.179 Ours FVD LPIPS PSNR SSIM 22.95 22.53 26.52 0.846 0.881 0. Method 57.44 7 Figure 5: Zero-shot human-to-robot video transfer on the H&R benchmark. DreamX preserves the source motion and target robot appearance, while the baselines exhibit visual degradation or human-hand leakage. AdaWorld exhibits visual degradation in this out-of-distribution setting, while VideoWorld 2 occasionally introduces human hand despite its appearance-disentangling design. These results suggest that DreamX better separates transferable motion from appearance, enabling more consistent human-to-robot transfer. 4.3 ACTION TRANSFER We evaluate action transfer to examine whether our latent actions form universal representation space that connects similar motions across embodiments. Following Sec. 3.3, we extract latent actions from human video and decode them into low-level actions for the target robot. Execution is open-loop without visual observations: only the latent actions specify the motion, while proprioception provides the robots initial state. Notably, this transfer is learned without paired humanrobot training data, so the two embodiments are connected through the shared latent action space. Figure 6 shows that the robot reproduces the stroke structure of the letter N, preserving the demonstrated motion beyond coarse task outcome. In single-arm pushing, it follows the forward-thenleft sequence, retaining the direction change and temporal order. Bimanual pushing further shows corresponding movements of both arms, suggesting that the shared latent representation retains armspecific motion and transfers it to the corresponding robot arms. Evaluation protocols and additional examples are provided in Appendices B.2 and D.2, respectively. 4.4 POLICY EVALUATION We conduct real-world drawer-closing study to examine whether DreamXs learned latent actions can support downstream policy learning. Given the instruction close the drawer, the robot must close the upper drawer, the lower drawer, or both sequentially. We compare DreamX with Mimic-Video (Pai et al., 2025), both trained using human videos and robot demonstrations. During rollout, Mimic-Video generates future video, while DreamX generates compact latent actions alongside low-level actions. Table 4 shows that action supervision slightly improves regression MSE from 0.24 to 0.23, while classification accuracy slightly decreases from 65.3% to 64.8%. We examine whether latent actions guide the motion reconstructed by the decoder. Keeping the initial frame and sampling noise fixed, we perturb the latent actions or replace them with zeros. In Figure 7, the original latent actions reconstruct the grasping and lifting motion, whereas perturbation disrupts object manipulation and zeroing largely suppresses motion. The surrounding scene remains largely unchanged, supporting the role of latent actions in specifying motion beyond appearance. Quantitative results are provided in Appendix C.3. 9 Figure 7: Sensitivity analysis. Perturbing latent actions alters motion while preserving scene appearance. Figure 8: Query-to-video attention. To examine where DreamX reads motion information, Figure 8 visualizes query-to-video attention during latent-action encoding of human and robot demonstrations. Attention highlights the hands and grippers involved in object interactions, suggesting that the queries read action-relevant regions across embodiments. Additional visualizations are provided in Appendix D.4.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present DreamX, framework that leverages pretrained video diffusion priors to learn universal latent actions. Its spatiotemporal representations provide action-relevant dynamics, while its generative prior supervises latent-action learning through future-frame reconstruction. DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models on LARYBench and enables any-to-any video transfer and human-to-robot action transfer without paired training data. Predicting these compact latent actions also supports effective and efficient policy learning from human and robot demonstrations. Together, these results highlight pretrained video models as foundation for learning reusable action representations across embodiments.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: All datasets used in this work are publicly available, including the human egocentric and robot demonstration datasets listed in Appendix A.1. Human videos may contain identifiable people or surroundings, so any redistributed examples should follow the source datasets usage terms and privacy requirements. Video-transfer outputs are synthetic and should be identified as such. Crossembodiment transfer and robot policies may fail outside the evaluated settings and require safety validation before deployment. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT Section 3 describes the model, training objectives, transfer procedure, and policy. Appendix documents the data sources and implementation details, while Appendix specifies the benchmark, transfer, and real-world policy evaluation protocols. Supplementary videos illustrate video-transfer and action-transfer results; policy rollouts are provided in Appendix D.3.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 TRAINING DATA We pretrain DreamX on 2.19k hours of human and robot video spanning six datasets (Figure 9). Human demonstrations contribute 469 hours from EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2026) and EgoVerse (Punamiya et al., 2026), complementing robot demonstrations from Bridge (Walke et al., 2023), DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024), AgiBot (Bu et al., 2025a), and MolmoAct-BimanualYAM (Fang et al., 2026). A.2 DREAMX PRETRAINING We initialize DreamX from Cosmos-Predict2.5 2B and train at 480 640 resolution for 78,000 steps. Training clips contain 529 frames in increments of four, corresponding to 28 VAE latent frames. We assign four query tokens to each latent frame, yielding up to 32 query tokens per clip. The encoder and decoder use separate rank-16 LoRA modules, while the pretrained backbone weights remain frozen. Learning rates are 104 for the LoRA parameters and query embeddings and 5 105 for the remaining trainable parameters, with 500 warm-up steps. Video and action losses receive equal weights for action-labeled clips; clips without action labels use only the video loss. A.3 LATENT-ACTION COMPRESSION We train variational bottleneck on latent actions extracted by the frozen DreamX encoder. Following (Gao et al., 2026), the bottleneck compresses each token from backbone width to while preserving the token layout. 14 Figure 9: Pretraining data composition. DreamX learns from six datasets spanning human and robot demonstrations. Sector areas represent video duration, with human datasets highlighted in warm colors. Formulation. The encoder fψ parameterizes factorized Gaussian posterior qψ(Z Q) through (cid:0)µψ(Q), log σ2 ψ(Q)(cid:1) = fψ(Q). We compute the reconstruction loss in fixed normalized feature space. Architecture and Training. The bottleneck encoder uses single self-attention block to produce 32-dimensional code for each 2,048-dimensional latent-action token. six-layer transformer decoder reconstructs the original features. The token layout is preserved: for 32-token input, the bottleneck maps 32 2,048 representation to 32 32 compact codes. We train the bottleneck for 50,000 steps with learning rate of 104, 500 warm-up steps, and KL weight of β = 0.01. After training, we freeze the bottleneck and use the posterior mean, to obtain deterministic compact codes for downstream policy learning and evaluation. = µψ(Q), A.4 POLICY TRAINING AND INFERENCE To convert the pretrained video model into latent-action generator, we train it to predict compact latent-action codes conditioned on the current observation and language instruction. We use approximately one-third of the DreamX pretraining data and optimize rank-128 LoRA modules in self-attention, cross-attention, and feed-forward layers, together with trainable input and output projections. The generator is trained for 100,000 steps on two NVIDIA H200 GPUs with global batch size of 60, learning rate of 104, and 1,000 warm-up steps. The Action DiT is not separately pretrained; it is introduced during task-specific policy learning and trained jointly with the generator. Task-specific training settings are provided in Appendix B.3.

sections.title: B EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND EVALUATION PROTOCOLS
sections.content: B.1 REAL-WORLD ROBOT SETUP We conduct both action-transfer and policy experiments on bimanual YAM robot. The action space consists of 14dimensional absolute commands, comprising six joint positions and one gripper command per arm. We leverage one Intel RealSense D405 camera for observation, which is mounted on top view. B.2 ACTION TRANSFER DETAILS Figure 10: BimanualYAM setup. We extract latent actions from human demonstrations using the frozen DreamX encoder and decode them into robot commands. The resulting trajectory is executed open-loop, without visual feedback, conditioned on the human latent actions and the robots initial proprioceptive state. We evaluate three types of motion transfer. Writing tests whether latent actions preserve finegrained spatial trajectories and stroke order; marker attached to the right gripper reproduces the demonstrated shape. Single-arm pushing tests whether the representation captures changes in motion direction and their temporal order, requiring the robot to follow forward-then-left sequence. Bimanual manipulation tests whether latent actions retain arm-specific motion and transfer it to the corresponding robot arms. Additional examples are provided in Section D.2. B.3 POLICY EVALUATION DETAILS Task and observations. We evaluate three drawer-closing configurations: only the upper drawer open, only the lower drawer open, and both drawers open, as illustrated in Figure 11. All configurations use the instruction close the drawer. When both drawers are open, the robot must close the upper drawer before the lower drawer. fixed top-view RGB camera observes the workspace. (a) Upper drawer open (b) Lower drawer open (c) Both drawers open Figure 11: Real-world drawer-closing setup. Initial observations for the three task configurations, all conditioned on close the drawer. When both drawers are open, the robot must close the upper drawer before the lower drawer. Training. We compare DreamX with Mimic-Video (Pai et al., 2025), using human videos and robot demonstrations for task-specific learning. DreamX starts from the pretrained latent-action generator, while Mimic-Video starts from video backbone pretrained on MolmoAct. Each method then incorporates an action head for task-specific learning, and both are trained for 30,000 steps. For DreamX, human videos supervise latent-action prediction, while robot demonstrations additionally supervise low-level actions. During rollout, DreamX generates compact latent actions alongside low-level actions, whereas Mimic-Video generates future video. Evaluation. We evaluate reaching and pushing as two subgoals: reaching measures whether the robot approaches the drawer for interaction, and pushing measures whether it completes the required closure. The reported subgoal success rate averages the two completion rates within each configuration, and the overall average weights the three configurations equally. We additionally report inference latency per policy call. Separate reaching and pushing results are provided in Section C.1. We collected 45 trajectories to train the policy and evaluated its success rate over 10 trials in each of three scenarios. 16 B.4 LARYBENCH EVALUATION DETAILS Evaluation protocol. We freeze all representation models and train common attentive probe for action regression and classification. Each input token is projected to 768 dimensions through linear layer, layer normalization, and GELU. For representations spanning multiple transitions, learned temporal embeddings identify the transition positions before the temporal and token dimensions are flattened. learned-query attentive pooler aggregates the tokens into single feature for the regression or classification head. Feature extraction. The regression benchmark originally provides only two frames per sample. Using the accompanying metadata, we recover the corresponding video sequences from the source datasets, including the intervening frames, for video-based models. We extract each models native representation without fine-tuning and preserve its temporal and token structure. Pair-based models encode consecutive frame pairs, while video-based models encode clips using their supported temporal windows. Features are precomputed for probe training. B.5 ZERO-SHOT HUMAN-TO-ROBOT TRANSFER DETAILS We evaluate on 1,008 clips spanning 21 tasks from HumanAndRobot (Xie et al., 2026), selecting 48 clips per task. Each method receives human source video and the initial frame of its paired robot recording. The remaining robot frames serve only as evaluation references; no paired humanrobot data is used for training. We compare DreamX with AdaWorld (Gao et al., 2025) and VideoWorld 2 (Ren et al., 2026b) using their native generation horizons. For common evaluation horizon, we retain the first 20 frames of each output and exclude the conditioning frame, yielding 19 generated frames per clip. We report FVD using Kinetics-400pretrained I3D network, VGG-based LPIPS, PSNR, and SSIM against the corresponding robot reference videos.
